parole.testo: Attested since 1130-40 as brazda. From South Slavic brazda, from Proto-Slavic *borzda.

Attested since 1532. Morphologically as bazsa (“peony”) + rózsa (“rose”). The first member of the compound is shortened from Old Hungarian bazsar (“peony”) (1470), borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *božurъ (“peony”).
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *byvolъ.

parole.significato: ban (title in the historical Kingdom of Croatia and the Kingdom of Hungary, like a palatine or governor of a province)
parole.testo: From Old Hungarian ban (1146), from a South Slavic language; compare Serbo-Croatian bȃn/ба̑н (“lord; ban”), from Proto-Slavic *banъ; see there for more.

parole.significato: vat, bucket, pail (a round container with one handle, made of wood or tin, used to carry liquids)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic or West Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *čьbьrъ.
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, from Latin cerrus. Compare Serbo-Croatian cer (“Turkey oak”).
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *čerpъ.
Borrowed from a South Slavic language. Compare Slovene četrtek, Bulgarian четвъртък (četvărtăk), Serbo-Croatian četvrtak. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *četvьrtъkъ, from *četvьrtъ (“fourth”).

parole.significato: expensive (having a high price or cost)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic or a West Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian, Slovene drag; Czech, Slovak drahý; Polish drogi (“expensive, dear”), from Proto-Slavic *dorgъ. Hungarian most likely borrowed the feminine form of the Slavic adjective.

parole.significato: grain, crop (harvested seeds of various grass-related food crops)
parole.testo: Borrowed from South Slavic, found in Old Church Slavonic гобино (gobino, “crops, harvest, abundance”), cognate to Lithuanian Gabjaujis, Gabjaujaᵂᴾ, Latvian Gabjauja (“the god of agriculture”).

parole.significato: clove (any one of the separate bulbs that make up the larger bulb of garlic)
parole.testo: First attested in 1395. Borrowed from a South Slavic language. Compare Bulgarian грозд (grozd, “bunch of grapes”), dialectal Bulgarian грезд (grezd, “spigot”), Serbo-Croatian grozd (“[bunch of] grapes”), Slovene grȍzd (“id.”), Old Church Slavonic гроздъ (grozdŭ, “id.”).
Borrowed from a South Slavic language + -ol. Compare Serbo-Croatian gaziti (“to wade”).
From the dialectal and literary variant kondor (“curly”), a loanword from a South Slavic language. Compare Slovene koder.
Borrowed from South Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *guna, *guňa (“coarse fur garment”). First attested in 1388.
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *xvala.
Borrowed from a South Slavic or West Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian hrčak.

parole.significato: leader or village judge of Romanian or Ruthenian settler communities
parole.testo: Borrowed from South Slavic languages. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kъnędzь. First attested in 1055.
Borrowed from a South Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian krst (“cross”) and Bulgarian кръст (krăst). From Proto-Slavic *krьstъ.

parole.significato: king (a male monarch; member of a royal family who is the supreme ruler of his nation)
parole.testo: Borrowed from South Slavic, probably from Serbo-Croatian. Cognate with contemporary Serbo-Croatian krȃlj, Slovene králj, Turkish kral, Bulgarian крал (kral), Slovak kráľ, from Proto-Slavic *korľь (“king”), itself from Old High German Karl, the name of the Frankish ruler Charlemagne.

parole.significato: basket (round lightweight container, especially one that is woven)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian košara, Slovene košara. The meaning “rejection” came into use in analogy with German Korb (“basket; rejection”), which in turn is due to a medieval custom of giving a bottomless basket as a symbol of unrequited love.

parole.significato: steward (a person in charge of buildings, grounds, etc.)
parole.testo: From a South Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian ključar. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *kľučь; compare with kulcs (“key”).

parole.significato: cooper (maker of wooden barrels and similar vessels)
parole.testo: Probably from a South Slavic language or Slovak kadár. Compare dialectal Slovene kadar (“cooper”). Probably from Proto-Slavic *kadъ (“tub”). The noun kádár is definitely not from the noun kád (“tub”) because the suffix -ár is characteristic in words created during the Hungarian language reform, whic

First attested in c. 1325. Borrowed from South Slavic. Compare Old Church Slavonic лѧща (lęšta), Bulgarian леща (lešta), Macedonian леќа (leḱa), Serbo-Croatian leća, Slovene leča. First used in the sense of plant. Later, after German influence, it also emerged as a medical term (in anatomy) [1787] a
First attested in the 15th century. Borrowed from a South Slavic or a West Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian lug, Slovene lug.
Borrowed from South Slavic or Slovak močiar. Compare Serbo-Croatian močvara.

parole.significato: fluke, trematode (a parasitic flatworm of the Trematoda class)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic language. Compare Bulgarian метил (metil), Serbo-Croatian metilj (“fluke”).

parole.significato: bed (a piece of furniture on which to rest or sleep)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian nosila (“stretcher”), Bulgarian носи́ло (nosílo, “stretcher”).

parole.significato: nanny (usually a young woman who takes care of other people’s young)
parole.testo: Probably borrowed from a South Slavic language. Compare dialectal Slovene pestrnja (“nanny”).

Probably borrowed from a South Slavic or West Slavic language, compare Bulgarian пичка (pička), Slovak pička, and Polish piczka. The form in Hungarian was created from an erroneously inferred Slavic root.

parole.significato: a type of small round cake, similar to a kind of scone
parole.testo: Via a South Slavic language, ultimately from the feminine form of Latin focācius (“of the hearth, baked on a fire”), from Latin focus (“hearth, fireplace”). Compare Serbo-Croatian pogača (“unleavened bread”), Bulgarian погача (pogača), Macedonian погача (pogača, “unleavened bread”). Cognates in Roma

parole.significato: bailiff (servant of the law, usually a lay person, who acted as an officer and a public witness during oral proceedings…
parole.testo: Borrowed from South Slavic, ultimately from Old Church Slavonic приставъ (pristavŭ). Compare zászló and boroszlán for the sound change /st/ > /sl/. Compare Romanian pristav. First attested in 1200.
Borrowed from a South Slavic language, perhaps from Serbo-Croatian ра̏б /rȁb, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *orbъ.

parole.significato: frying pan, skillet (long-handled, shallow pan used for frying food)
parole.testo: Of debated origin: # Borrowed from South Slavic, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *čerpъ. # Borrowed from German, possibly based on Middle High German *scherpene pfanne (“clay skillet”).

parole.significato: bacon (salt cured and smoked, that can be eaten without cooking)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic or West Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian slanina.

parole.significato: sweepings, litter (collectively, items discarded on the ground)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic or West Slavic language. Compare Bulgarian смет (smet), Serbo-Croatian smȅt.
Borrowed from a South Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian sreća, Slovene sreča (“luck, happiness”), from Proto-Slavic *sъręťa; see Proto-Slavic *sъrě̀sti (“to meet, encounter”) for more.

parole.significato: to walk, stroll (to wander on foot; to walk leisurely)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian šetati. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *šętati. With -l + [Term?] (verb-forming suffix).
Borrowed from a South Slavic or West Slavic language.
Borrowed from a South Slavic or West Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian talog.
Borrowed from a South Slavic language. Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *tyky.

Borrowed from a South Slavic language. Compare Bulgarian витез (vitez), Serbo-Croatian vitez (“knight, warrior”), from Proto-Slavic *vitędzь, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *wīkingaz (compare Old Norse víkingr).
From a South Slavic language. Compare Serbo-Croatian zob.

parole.significato: any flowering plant of the genus Althaea
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic or West Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *slězъ (“mallow”) (compare Serbo-Croatian сље̏з /sljȅz (“mallow”), Czech sléz (“mallow”), Slovak slez (“mallow”), Slovene slẹ̑z (“mallow”)). Possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European [Term?], compare Old High German slihhan (

From a South Slavic or West Slavic language, compare Serbo-Croatian zuvor, Slovene zavor, Czech závora, Slovak závor, Polish zawór, Old Church Slavonic заворъ (zavorŭ), завора (zavora), from Proto-Slavic *za- + *vorъ (compare *zaverti), with equivalents in East Slavic languages (such as Russian затв
Borrowed from a South Slavic language or from Slovak hrable. Compare Serbo-Croatian grablje.

parole.significato: dam (a structure placed across a flowing body of water to stop the flow or part of the flow)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic language, e.g. Serbo-Croatian gat, or from Slovak hať. Ultimately, from Proto-Slavic *gatь (“dike”).

parole.significato: ear, spike (the fruiting body of a grain plant)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a South Slavic language or from Slovak klas, from Proto-Slavic *kolsъ.
Borrowed either from a South Slavic language or from Slovak mrena, ultimately from Proto-Slavic *merna. First attested in 1590.

From either South Slavic or East Slavic, from Old Church Slavonic сѫбота (sǫbota), from Byzantine Greek *σάμβατον (*sámbaton), from Ancient Greek σάββατον (sábbaton), from Hebrew שַׁבָּת (šabbāṯ). The borrowing occurred in the eleventh century during the Christianization of the Hungarians, and befor
Borrowed from a South Slavic language or from Slovak. Its original form was ugorka. Compare Slovak uhorka.

parole.significato: to practice magic, do things by magic
parole.testo: From a South Slavic language or from Slovak. Compare Serbo-Croatian vražiti⁽ˢʰ⁾ and Slovak vražiť (“to practice sorcery/magic/black art”), presumably from Proto-Slavic *vorgъ.
